extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Step 2A (first part of the Alice/Mayo two-part test) patent-eligibility analysis under 35 U.S.C. §101, including how to identify judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) and when claims directed to improvements in computer functionality are not abstract. Focuses on claim construction (BRI), identifying claimed concept(s), comparison to precedent, and examiner practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI covering statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter (Step 1: NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. It is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to embodiments that fall within a statutory category. Example: machine-readable-media claims whose BRI encompasses transitory carrier waves (see In re Nuijten and Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA). If applicant disclosure suggests the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, the analysis may proceed to whether an amended claim would be eligible (Pathway A/B/C), and the examiner should recommend such an amendment where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject clear non-statutory claims at Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) (Step 1: NO), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating the claim is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., 7.05 and 7.05.01) and MPEP §706.03(a). However, if the specification suggests the claim could be amended to be statutory, proceed to analyze such an amended claim's eligibility and recommend amendment as a best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to nothing more than abstract ideas (e.g., mathematical algorithms), laws of nature, and natural phenomena are not eligible for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have described these exceptions with various overlapping terms (physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied concepts). There are no bright lines between exception types; it is sufficient for analysis to identify that the claimed concept aligns with at least one judicial exception. See MPEP §2106.04(a)/(b) for detailed discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption is the underlying concern but not a standalone test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's concern about judicial exceptions is preemption (that monopolization of these basic tools would impede innovation), but preemption is not a separate, standalone test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of preemption are inherent in and are resolved by applying the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B). Examiners should apply the Alice/Mayo test rather than rely on preemption alone. Case examples indicate preemption should be considered but evaluated via the two-step analysis (e.g., Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A core inquiry — does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A asks whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea. A claim is 'directed to' a judicial exception when such an exception is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Recite’ covers different ways an exception can appear: it can be explicitly set forth (e.g., Diehr’s mathematical equation in a claim step), included in a wherein clause (Mayo), or described conceptually (Alice described intermediated settlement without using the exact words). Treat the claim as a whole when performing Step 2A. If Step 2A: NO (not directed to an exception), the claim is eligible at Pathway B. If Step 2A: YES, proceed to Step 2B to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reciting an exception from merely involving one
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must distinguish claims that recite an exception (which require further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception (which are eligible and do not require further analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example reciting an exception: 'A machine comprising elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' (recites law of nature -> Step 2A: YES). Example merely involving an exception: a teeter-totter claim that is based on the law of the lever but does not recite the natural principle (-> Step 2A: NO). Evaluate the claim as a whole and focus on whether the exception is actually set forth in claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not improperly parse or split a recited exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless distinct, examiners should not parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions; related concepts (e.g., manipulation of information through a series of mental steps) should be considered a single abstract idea for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if a claim does recite multiple distinct exceptions (even if related), it is directed to at least one judicial exception and requires Step 2B analysis. See RecogniCorp v. Nintendo for an example where multiple abstract ideas were treated as a single abstract idea and subjected to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to identify abstract ideas (two-step approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea, examiners should (1) identify the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) believed to be an abstract idea), and (2) compare that concept to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to concepts previously identified as abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude the concept is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES), requiring Step 2B analysis. If it is not similar and no basis exists to treat it as an abstract idea, the claim is not directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B unless another exception is recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to improvements in computer functionality/technology are not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inventions that pertain to improvements in computer functionality or other technologies are not abstract when appropriately claimed and therefore may be eligible at Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key considerations: the specification should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement; the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology; evaluate under the BRI and consider whether the claim covers a particular solution or way to achieve a desired outcome rather than merely the idea of a solution. See Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory for examples where claims were found not directed to abstract ideas because they focused on specific improvements. See also MPEP §2106.05(a) for more guidance and contrasting cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does NOT qualify as an improvement to computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere automation of manual processes, performance improvements that arise solely from using a general-purpose computer, claims that can be performed without a computer, or claims that merely implement an idea on generic components do not show an improvement in computer functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/cases: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (method performable mentally; not an improvement in a computer), FairWarning IP v. Iatric Systems and Credit Acceptance v. Westlake (mere automation or speed by generic computers insufficient), Affinity Labs and TLI Communications (claims using conventional implementation on generic components insufficient). Examiners should look for more than conventional implementation on generic machinery to find an improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve improvement question early where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are encouraged to resolve whether a claim reflects an improvement to computer-related technology as early as possible in the eligibility analysis (Step 2A or even Pathway A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear improvement (e.g., Enfish) could justify finding eligibility at Pathway A under a streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. If the improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may still contribute to the Step 2B analysis. Examiners should evaluate specification and claim together under the BRI to determine whether an improvement is present.
